1.1.1 Assessments:
This is the first of three lab weeks (weeks 2, 3 and 4) where the data you collect will be used for your first professional report assessment (1-page report in week 9). HELPFUL TIP: The more attention you pay to the quality of your data during this lab, the easier it will be to complete your professional.


1.1.2 Background:
Maximal sprinting speed and its derivative acceleration have both been shown to be key discriminators in playing status across many sports. Whilst, performing a maximal sprint test would give the most valid insight into these qualities, it may not always be possible to perform this test in a practical environment due factors such as, perceived risk of injury and cost of equipment (timing gates, radar gun etc). Hence, identifying cost effective test that may give insight into these qualities is of interest.
Two commonly used test that are used as both proxy measures of acceleration and sprinting speed respectively are the standing broad jump (SBJ) and assessment of lower limb stiffness. Whilst a number of techniques for measuring lower limb stiffness exist, the test we will focus on today is the drop jump test.
PART 1 of today will involve collecting data across a 0-5 and 0-10m sprint test, standing broad jump and drop jump test (look to get at least two trials across each test). PART 2 aims of today involve calculating basic summary statistics that represent the mean and spread/deviation of the data and other descriptive statistics discussed in the lecture.

2.3.1 Bland-Altman plot
One of the key ways we look to assess the ability to interchange between testing technologies that are attempting to measure the same trait is use of a Bland-Altman plot.
We will discuss Bland-Altman plots in more detail in the lecture in Week 4 but quite simply all the Bland-Altman plot attempts to show us is the difference between one test compared to another test measuring the same thing/
For example we might compare jump height collected from a force plate and linear position transducer. From this we are interested in knowing the mean difference between measures (BIAS) and limits of agreement (LOA). LOA is calculated by looking at the standard deviation of the differences between test and multiplying by 2 (technically 1.96).

The ULOA is then BIAS + LOA
and
LLOA calculated as BIAS - LOA

2.5.2 Visual 2
The visual below looks to highlight the importance of wanting to minimise Typical Error. You hopefully feel comfortable with the idea that any measurement we collect has some uncertainty around it. That uncertainty may be due to biological variation, technology and or methodology error, which all limit our confidence in reporting a “true” measurement. We aim to represent this uncertainty in a similar fashion to what we did last week with the 95% Confidence Interval (CI).
To calculate the CI around the observed scores (point A and B), we use a similar formula that we did last week when we calculated the 95% CI around a sample mean, the only difference being instead of using a standard error, we will use the Typical Error (TE).
For example,
Point A score = 50. For a given value of the Typical Error slider, e.g. 3 the 95 % CI would be
50 - (3 \(\times\) 1.96) = 44.1 to 50 + (3 \(\times\) 1.96) = 55.9
This interval represents our uncertainty around where we believe the true measurement might be. From an interpretation perspective we can’t say the probability of the true value being between the lower limit and upper limit is 95%, rather that the method we used to create the interval has a 95% success rate in capturing true values over the long run.
We can also calculate an uncertainty around the change score observed between these two measurements (A and B). Now that we are comparing two measurements that both come with uncertainty we have to adjust our calculation slightly to account for this when calculating a CI for a change score we do so with the equation below.
Change 95% LL = (Point B - Point A observed values) - \(\sqrt{2}\) \(\times\) TE \(\times\) 1.96 Change 95% UL = (Point B - Point A observed values) + \(\sqrt{2}\) \(\times\) TE \(\times\) 1.96
The \(\sqrt{2}\) is included because we now have two trials that both have a potential source of uncertainty. The addition of the \(\sqrt{2}\) as you can see makes the CI larger for change scores than for individual observations.

Two more measures we discussed in the lecture that can also be calculated from an understanding of TE are the minimal detectable change MDC and minimal clinically import difference MCID. Both of these are commonly reported to a 95% confidence level so will be multiplied by 1.96 respectively. The key take away is that the MDC is looking to tell you how the large the change would need to be for you to be confident at the 95% level that the observed change wasn’t due to measurement noise. However the MDC only tells you whether a change is statistically different from zero which may not indicate that the change is meaningful in a practical sense. The MCID however, aims to let you know whether the change observed is greater than some magnitude of importance often termed the smallest worthwhile change (SWC).
MDC_95 = TE \(\times\) \(\sqrt{2}\) \(\times\) 1.96
MCID_95 = MDC_95 + SWC
Whilst there are may ways we can identify a value considered the SWC, a commonly used method is to multiply the between subject SD by some factor. In exercise and sport science a commonly used factor is 0.2 therefore;
SWCsml = SD \(\times\) 0.2 (Small)
SWCmdr = SD \(\times\) 0.6 (Moderate)
SWClrg = SD \(\times\) 1.2 (Large)

text:
2.6 Test your learning

What does a Bland-Altman plot show?

 The difference between measurements plotted against time The difference between measurements plotted against the mean of both measurements The correlation between two measurements The mean of both measurements plotted against time

What does the mean difference line (bias) in a Bland-Altman plot represent?

 Random error in the measurements The standard deviation of the differences Systematic differences between measurements The reliability of the measurement

What does the Typical Error (TE) represent?

 The average difference between measurements The typical variation in repeated measurements for an individual The minimum detectable change The correlation between measurements

If you have a single measurement (e.g., 45 kg) and know the Typical Error (TE) is 2 kg, how would you construct a 95% confidence interval around this measurement?

 Add and subtract 1×TE from the measurement Add and subtract 1.96×TE from the measurement Add and subtract 2×TE from the measurement Add and subtract the MDC95 from the measurement

If you measure an athlete’s max strength as 80 kg with a TE of 3 kg and calculate a 95% confidence interval of 74.1-85.9 kg, what does this interval represent?

 The athlete will score between 74.1-85.9 kg on 95% of future tests 95% of athletes with similar measured strength have a true strength in this range If we could measure this athlete's strength at this exact moment repeatedly without fatigue, 95% of the confidence intervals calculated using the above procedure would contain their true strength The athlete's strength will improve by up to 5.9 kg or decrease by up to 5.9 kg with 95% probability

What does the Minimum Detectable Change (MDC95) represent?

 The smallest change that could occur by chance The average change between measurements The minimum change needed to be confident a real change has occurred at the 95% confidence level The typical error multiplied by 0.68

When monitoring an individual’s changes over time, which criterion should you use to determine if a real change has occurred?

 The change is significant if it exceeds the TE The change is significant if it exceeds the MDC95 The change is significant if it exceeds the mean bias The change is significant if it exceeds the CV

Why is the Coefficient of Variation (CVTE%) useful?

 It allows comparison of reliability between different units It expresses error relative to the mean It's useful when error increases with larger values All of the above

If you want to construct a 95% confidence interval around an individual’s measurement, you should use:

 ±1 × TE from the measured value ±1.96 × TE from the measured value ±1 × MDC from the measured value ±2 × CV from the measured value

4.4 Task 1:
Over the last 5 weeks we have learnt about concepts relating to descriptive statistics, validity, reliability and dose response relationships. In particular, a focus a was made regarding the importance of reliability and how it can help identify was can be considered a practically meaningful effect.
In the first task, your tutor will rotate you in pairs. One of you will act as the client and one of you will act as the trainer. The trainer, using the interactive document below is to draw a random sample of data, and then summarise the data to their partner as if they were a client.
https://r2mu.github.io/ETM_Wk5/






Example





Mean 1-RM squat: 120 kg and Standard deviation (SD): 15 kg Test-retest reliability showed a SD of difference scores = 5.66 kg
Calculations:
Typical Error (TE) = SD_diff/√2 = 5.66/1.414 = 4 kg
CVTE = 4/120*100 = 3.33%
Interpretation: On average, repeated measurements will vary by about 4 kg due to measurement variability.

Minimal Detectable Change (MDC) = TE×√2×1.96 = 4×1.414×1.96 = 11.1 kg
Interpretation: A change of at least 11.1 kg is needed to be 95% confident the change is real and not due to measurement error.

Smallest Worthwhile Change (SWC) = 0.2×SD = 0.2×15 = 3 kg
Interpretation: A change of 3 kg would be considered practically meaningful for these athletes.

Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) = MDC+SWC = 11.1+3 = 14.1 kg
Interpretation: An increase of at least 14.1 kg represents a change that is both statistically significant and practically meaningful.

Why do we calculate a z-score?

 To calculate the mean of a distribution To determine the sample size needed for a study To standardize values so they can be compared across different scales and distributions To convert all negative values to positive values

A student scores 85 on a fitness test where the class mean is 75 and the standard deviation is 6.67. What is their z-score? (Round to 1 decimal place)

 -0.5 1.5 2.5 0.67

In the linear regression equation y = mx + b, which statement correctly describes the relationship?

 y equals the sum of x and b y equals the product of x and m, minus b y equals the product of m and x, plus b y equals the sum of m and x, divided by b

In a linear regression equation y = mx + b, what does the slope (m) represent?

 The value of y when the analysis begins The amount y changes when x increases by one unit The starting point of the regression line The amount x changes when y increases by one unit

In a linear regression equation y = mx + b, what does the y-intercept (b) represent?

 The average value of all y measurements The point where the regression line crosses the x-axis The predicted value of y when x equals zero The minimum possible value for y in the dataset

What does Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) represent in the context of linear regression?

 The proportion of variance in y explained by x The average error in the prediction model The slope of the regression line The strength and direction of the linear relationship between x and y

What does the coefficient of determination (R²) represent in linear regression?

 The square root of the average squared error The square of the slope in the regression equation The proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable The average distance between predicted and actual values

What does the standard error of the estimate represent in linear regression?

 The average distance of data points from the mean The average distance between observed values and predicted values on the regression line The standard deviation of the slope coefficient The standard deviation of the x variable

If a regression equation is TestScore = 2x + 65, where x is hours spent studying, what is the correct interpretation if a student increases their study time from 10 to 15 hours?

 5 additional hours of studying has no effect on test scores 5 additional hours of studying is associated with a 10-point increase in test scores Each hour of studying is associated with a 2-point increase in test scores For every 2 points increase in test scores, students study 1 additional hour

If Pearson’s r = 0.8 for the relationship between two variables, what does the corresponding R² = 0.64 tell us?

 The relationship is perfectly linear There is no relationship between the variables About 64% of the variation in y can be explained by its linear relationship with x The slope of the regression line is 0.8

What does a Pearson’s r value of -0.7 indicate about the relationship between variables x and y?

title: 7  Week 12 - Practical
text:
7.5 But what is a p-value
A p-value can be thought of as the probability of observing the test statistic we did assuming that there is no difference between testing occasions. Put differently, that any effect you observed is explained via pure random sampling variation. Effectively, all we are doing when we calculate a p-value is comparing the test statistic we observed to a distribution of test statistics that can be created via random sampling variation. If we observe a test statistic that can very rarely be created under random sampling variation, let’s say less than 5% of the time, we deem this a statistically significant result. That is, we observed a test statistic that is very rarely observed under the null hypothesis so we will treat our result as interesting.
The simulation below will hopefully build your intuition around the null distribution and p-values.
https://r2mu.github.io/tvalSim/

7.5.1 What a p-value isn’t

Represent the probability that the null hypothesis is true

A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true, not the probability of the null being true

Measure the size, importance, or practical significance of an effect

Small p-values can occur with trivial effects in large samples, and large p-values can occur with important effects in small samples

Does not tell you the probability that your results occurred by chance alone

The p-value tells you how often you would observe results at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true (pure chance) - Remember we are assuming it is true.
It doesn’t tell you the probability that your specific result was caused by chance versus a real effect

Indicate the probability of replicating your finding

A significant result (p < .05) does not mean there’s a 95% chance of replication; replication probability depends on many other factors (sample size and size of the effect)

7.4 Hypothesis testing recap
A quick recap of the main points discussed in lecture material. When we perform a hypothesis test, we are effectively trying to identify whether the signal (mean difference) we have observed can be considered an interesting result or could easily be explained via random variation. For this unit, we are going to focus on the T-statistic calculated from a paired t-test design (effectively comparing the same individuals pre and post some intervention). The T-statistic is calculated as:
\[
T = \frac{\text{mean diff}}{\frac{\text{sd(differences)}}{\sqrt{N}}}
\]
Where \(N\) the number of participants.
Let’s look into the equation in a little more detail:
We have a mean difference which can be thought of as a signal. We divide that by the \(sd(differences)\), which can be thought of as the level of consistency in change amongst individuals or also considered a measure of noise
The smaller the noise (greater consistency), the larger the T-value will be.
Finally, we divide this noise by the \(\sqrt{N}\), which can be thought of as a penalty for the fact that we are only testing on a sample and not the full population
The more people, the less penalty is applied and the greater the T-value will be

You may then ask the question, “but do we care if something is only different than zero?”. Indeed, this is a perfectly reasonable question to ask and something that statisticians have been encouraging researchers to do for a long time and this is to report the magnitude of the effect. It should be noted that the word “magnitude” may mean different things in different contexts across different fields. However, the two measures of effect magnitude that I want you to focus on for this unit are

title: 6  Week 10 - Practical
text:
6.4 A worked example

6.4.1 The experience
Think about sessions you’ve done with short, sharp shuttles — lots of turning, stopping and starting. Your heart rate was high, your legs were burning, but you barely covered any distance. Now think about a long steady run — heaps of metres covered but it felt relatively comfortable.
If distance tells us how hard a session was, why doesn’t it match how it felt?



6.4.2 Changing speed costs energy
A moving body has kinetic energy. To change speed — speeding up or slowing down — energy must be either added to or removed from the system.
\[
KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2
\]
The \(v^2\) is important — each additional m/s of speed costs progressively more energy. Let’s work through it for a 75 kg athlete:
\[
0 \rightarrow 1 \text{ m/s}: \quad \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 75 \times 1^2 - \tfrac{1}{2} \times 75 \times 0^2 = 37.5 - 0 = \textbf{37.5 J}
\]
\[
1 \rightarrow 2 \text{ m/s}: \quad \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 75 \times 2^2 - \tfrac{1}{2} \times 75 \times 1^2 = 150 - 37.5 = \textbf{112.5 J}
\]
\[
2 \rightarrow 3 \text{ m/s}: \quad \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 75 \times 3^2 - \tfrac{1}{2} \times 75 \times 2^2 = 337.5 - 150 = \textbf{187.5 J}
\]
Notice how the same 1 m/s increase costs progressively more energy — 37.5 J, then 112.5 J, then 187.5 J. That’s the \(v^2\) doing its work. This is why repeated accelerations are so demanding, and why short shuttles at moderate speeds cost more energy than the distance alone suggests.


6.4.3 Maintaining speed still costs energy
So acceleration is expensive. But what about when you’re just running at a steady pace — is that free? No.
Even without changing speed, the body burns fuel to maintain the running gait — muscles contracting, tendons loading, legs swinging every stride. The rate of fuel consumption (metabolic power, in W/kg) is:
\[
P_{met} = C_r \times v
\]
For example:
\[
P_{met} = 3.6 \text{ J/kg/m} \times 3.89 \text{ m/s} = \textbf{14.0 W/kg} \text{ at 14 km/h}
\]
Where \(C_r \approx 3.6\) J/kg/m is the energy cost of running on flat ground — about 3.6 joules per kilogram of body mass per metre covered. This is the baseline metabolic cost — it’s always present. HR reflects it even when speed isn’t changing. Think of it like a car on a motorway at constant speed: the engine is still burning fuel even though nothing is changing.


6.4.4 Deceleration costs energy too — but where does it go?
When you slow down, kinetic energy doesn’t vanish — conservation of energy tells us it has to go somewhere. But here’s the key: that energy doesn’t show up proportionally through the traditional metabolic pathways we typically monitor (HR, VO2). Instead, it’s largely dissipated as heat through structural deformation: muscles lengthening under load, tendons and connective tissue absorbing impact forces.


6.4.5 Interactive metabolic power calculator





  
    Shuttle Length30 m
    
  
  
    Target Speed14 km/h
    
  



  





  Notice the asymmetry: During acceleration, metabolic power rises steeply — the metabolic system is paying heavily for the increase in KE. During deceleration, it barely drops — even though the same magnitude of KE is being removed from the system. If that energy isn't being captured by the metabolic equation, where is it going? Into the structures — through eccentric muscle actions and tissue deformation. That missing cost is invisible to HR and VO2.




Acceleration: energy flows through chemical/metabolic pathways. Muscles produce force concentrically, ATP is consumed, O2 demand rises. The cardiovascular system pays — HR goes up.
Deceleration: energy is absorbed through structural/mechanical pathways. Muscles lengthen eccentrically, tissue deforms, energy becomes heat. The cardiovascular system barely registers it —HR stays low. But the muscles are absorbing real energy — and they’ll let you know about it tomorrow.
This is the same magnitude of energy involved in both directions, but the body handles it through different pathways. Producing force concentrically (accelerating) is metabolically expensive — muscle efficiency is only ~25%. Absorbing force eccentrically (decelerating) is metabolically cheap but structurally costly.
This is why Vanrenterghem et al. (2017) proposed thinking about training load along a physiological–biomechanical continuum. While it’s not technically correct to treat these as completely separate systems, some activities emphasise energy transfer through chemical/metabolic pathways, whilst others emphasise energy transfer through structural/mechanical pathways.
In today’s practical, you’ll experience three protocols that sit at different points on this continuum — and compare what your HR tells you versus what your legs tell you.






Think of it like a car





Accelerating: The fuel pump increases flow. The engine burns more fuel. The fuel gauge drops. In humans: the metabolic system pays. O2 demand rises, HR climbs. The body “burns fuel” to produce force.
Cruising: Steady fuel flow. Engine ticking over efficiently. In humans: baseline metabolic cost (\(C_r \times v\)). HR steady. This is the most efficient phase per metre covered.
Braking: The engine is barely working — almost no fuel consumed. But the brake pads absorb the kinetic energy as heat. The brake pads wear out. In humans: metabolic cost drops — HR doesn’t reflect it. But muscles absorb the KE eccentrically. Tissue takes the load.
The brake pad question: What happens to brake pads when you brake hard and often? They overheat. They wear down. Now imagine a session with 30 short shuttles — that’s 30 hard braking events. Each one requires the muscles to produce large eccentric forces to absorb kinetic energy. The structural cost accumulates — microdamage to muscle fibres, inflammation, soreness the next day. HR won’t tell you this happened. But your legs will.





6.4.6 A note on efficiency
Humans aren’t perfectly efficient energy converters, and the efficiency changes depending on the activity. Producing force concentrically (accelerating) is metabolically expensive - muscle efficiency is only ~25%. Absorbing force eccentrically (decelerating) is metabolically cheap but structurally costly. The same magnitude of energy is involved, but the body handles it through different pathways depending on the direction.

Braking: The engine is barely working — almost no fuel consumed. But the brake pads absorb the kinetic energy as heat. The brake pads wear out. In humans: metabolic cost drops — HR doesn’t reflect it. But muscles absorb the KE eccentrically. Tissue takes the load.
The brake pad question: What happens to brake pads when you brake hard and often? They overheat. They wear down. Now imagine a session with 30 short shuttles — that’s 30 hard braking events. Each one requires the muscles to produce large eccentric forces to absorb kinetic energy. The structural cost accumulates — microdamage to muscle fibres, inflammation, soreness the next day. HR won’t tell you this happened. But your legs will.




7.4.6 A note on efficiency
Humans aren’t perfectly efficient energy converters, and the efficiency changes depending on the activity. Producing force concentrically (accelerating) is metabolically expensive - muscle efficiency is only ~25%. Absorbing force eccentrically (decelerating) is metabolically cheap but structurally costly. The same magnitude of energy is involved, but the body handles it through different pathways depending on the direction.

title: 8  Week 12 - Practical
text:
8.4 Hypothesis testing recap
A quick recap of the main points discussed in lecture material. When we perform a hypothesis test, we are effectively trying to identify whether the signal (mean difference) we have observed can be considered an interesting result or could easily be explained via random variation. For this unit, we are going to focus on the T-statistic calculated from a paired t-test design (effectively comparing the same individuals pre and post some intervention). The T-statistic is calculated as:
\[
T = \frac{\text{mean diff}}{\frac{\text{sd(differences)}}{\sqrt{N}}}
\]
Where \(N\) the number of participants.
Let’s look into the equation in a little more detail:
We have a mean difference which can be thought of as a signal. We divide that by the \(sd(differences)\), which can be thought of as the level of consistency in change amongst individuals or also considered a measure of noise
The smaller the noise (greater consistency), the larger the T-value will be.
Finally, we divide this noise by the \(\sqrt{N}\), which can be thought of as a penalty for the fact that we are only testing on a sample and not the full population
The more people, the less penalty is applied and the greater the T-value will be

Key points from the plot above should be that increasing the sample size increases the precision/confidence we have in what the true mean difference is between the pre and post intervention which is shown by the smaller confidence interval around the change score. This can cause an issue in extremely large samples where tiny mean differences can be deemed “statistically significant” as we are effectively very confident that true mean difference from pre to post may indeed be greater than zero. You may then ask the question, “but do we care if something is only different than zero?”. Indeed, this is a perfectly reasonable question to ask and something that statisticians have been encouraging researchers to do for a long time and this is to report the magnitude of the effect. It should be noted that the word “magnitude” may mean different things in different contexts across different fields. However, the two measures of effect magnitude that I want you to focus on for this unit are
\[
Cohens D = \frac{\text{mean diff}}{\text{Pooled SD}}
\]
Where \(Pooled SD\) is the average \(SD\) across both pre and post trials.
For understanding of qualitative interpretation around the Cohens D numbers make sure to check out the Week 11 and 12 seminar material.
The other measure of effect I want you to develop some intition around is common language effect size (CLES) sometimes also called the probability of superiority
\[ CLES = \Phi\left(\frac{\text{mean diff}}{\text{sd diff}}\right) \]
Okay lets talk through this a little more slowly as there is a scary looking symbol in there. We first compute what is called the signal to noise ratio \((SNR)\) which is calculated via \(\frac{\text{mean diff}}{\text{sd diff}}\). This is then put into a function with a scary looking symbol \(\Phi(\text{SNR})\) however all this function does is convert the SNR into a probability for us. This probability can be thought of a randomly drawn person from this sample having a higher score vs lower score.

title: 8  Week 12 - Practical
text:
8.5 But what is a p-value
A p-value can be thought of as the probability of observing the test statistic we did assuming that there is no difference between testing occasions. Put differently, that any effect you observed is explained via pure random sampling variation. Effectively, all we are doing when we calculate a p-value is comparing the test statistic we observed to a distribution of test statistics that can be created via random sampling variation. If we observe a test statistic that can very rarely be created under random sampling variation, let’s say less than 5% of the time, we deem this a statistically significant result. That is, we observed a test statistic that is very rarely observed under the null hypothesis so we will treat our result as interesting.
The simulation below will hopefully build your intuition around the null distribution and p-values.
https://r2mu.github.io/tvalSim/

8.5.1 What a p-value isn’t

Represent the probability that the null hypothesis is true

A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true, not the probability of the null being true

Measure the size, importance, or practical significance of an effect

Small p-values can occur with trivial effects in large samples, and large p-values can occur with important effects in small samples

Does not tell you the probability that your results occurred by chance alone

The p-value tells you how often you would observe results at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true (pure chance) - Remember we are assuming it is true.
It doesn’t tell you the probability that your specific result was caused by chance versus a real effect

Indicate the probability of replicating your finding

A significant result (p < .05) does not mean there’s a 95% chance of replication; replication probability depends on many other factors (sample size and size of the effect)

title: 7  Week 11 - Practical
text:
8.1 Overview
This practical introduces students to the foundational assessment skills expected of an Accredited Exercise Scientist (AES) working within the ESSA scope of practice. The lab is structured around three integrated components: pre-exercise health screening, postural observation, and dynamic movement evaluation. By the end of the session, students will have practised administering the APSS, critically appraised the role and limitations of postural assessment, and begun designing their own general movement screening document.
Duration: 2–3 hours
Equipment: APSS forms (printed or digital), goniometer, inclinometer, plumb line or posture grid (optional), measuring tape, laptop/tablet with webcam (for technology-assisted station, optional), data recording sheets.

title: 7  Week 11 - Practical
text:
8.2 Learning Objectives
By the end of this practical, students should be able to:

Administer and interpret the Adult Pre-exercise Screening System (APSS) Stages 1 and 2.
Use the pre-screening process as an opportunity to build rapport, gather relevant health and activity history, and identify referral needs.
Describe the purpose and limitations of static postural observation, including the scope boundaries of an ESSA Accredited Exercise Scientist.
Select and justify appropriate static and dynamic movement assessments for a given client scenario.
Identify what they are specifically looking for in each assessment and why.
Measure joint range of motion using a goniometer and/or inclinometer and compare findings to normative values.
Critically evaluate how emerging technologies (e.g., machine learning-based pose estimation) may complement or replace traditional observational methods.

title: 7  Week 11 - Practical
text:
8.3 Part 1: Pre-Exercise Health Screening (30–40 minutes)

8.3.1 Background
Pre-exercise screening is a legal duty of care and a professional obligation for all ESSA-accredited practitioners. The Adult Pre-exercise Screening System (APSS), co-developed by ESSA, AUSactive, and Sports Medicine Australia (SMA), is the nationally recognised standard for identifying individuals who may be at higher risk of an adverse event during physical activity.
The APSS consists of two stages:

Stage 1 (Compulsory): A 7-item self-report questionnaire covering known diseases and signs/symptoms of disease. Any “yes” response directs the individual to seek guidance from a qualified health professional before commencing or significantly upgrading their exercise program.
Stage 2 (Recommended): Administered by an exercise professional, this stage involves measured risk factor data (e.g., resting blood pressure, blood lipid profile, waist circumference, BMI) and behavioural information (e.g., smoking status, physical activity level) to help tailor exercise prescription and establish a more detailed risk profile.



8.3.2 Activity 1.1: Administering the APSS
Working in pairs, students take turns playing the role of practitioner and client.
Instructions:

Introduce yourself and explain the purpose of the screening to your “client.” Use plain language — this is your opportunity to practise effective communication, a core ESSA competency.
Administer Stage 1 of the APSS. Record responses carefully.
Based on Stage 1 responses, determine whether your client is cleared to proceed or requires referral.
If cleared, proceed to Stage 2. Measure and record resting heart rate (palpation and/or HR monitor), resting blood pressure (auscultatory method with sphygmomanometer), and any other available Stage 2 measures.
Interpret the combined Stage 1 and 2 findings. What risk category does your client fall into? What does this mean for exercise prescription?

Key Discussion Points:

The APSS is a screening tool, not a diagnostic tool. An AES does not diagnose medical conditions.
Pre-screening is not just a form to tick off — it is your first opportunity to build rapport, understand the client’s goals, health history, injury history, current activity levels, and any concerns they bring.
Ask open-ended questions beyond the form: “Tell me about your current activity levels,” “Have you had any injuries or pain that affect how you move?”, “What are you hoping to get out of working with me?”
Consider: when do you need to refer, and to whom? Know the boundaries between an AES, an Accredited Exercise Physiologist (AEP), and a medical practitioner.



8.3.3 Scope of Practice Reminder
The ESSA AES Scope of Practice states that an AES can: “Screen and assess health, movement, exercise and performance capacity” and must “recognise the need to refer a client to other related professionals (e.g., Accredited Sports Scientists, Accredited Exercise Physiologists) as required.”
This means you can screen and identify risk factors, but you do not diagnose conditions, interpret pathology results beyond basic risk stratification, or manage clinical populations without appropriate referral or oversight.

title: 7  Week 11 - Practical
text:
8.4 Part 2: Static Postural Observation (20–30 minutes)

8.4.1 Background
Static postural observation has historically been a standard component of physical assessment in exercise science, physiotherapy, and sports settings. The traditional approach involves observing the client in standing from the anterior, posterior, and lateral views, using a plumb line or posture grid as a reference, and noting deviations from a theoretical “ideal” alignment.
However, students should understand several important caveats:
What the evidence actually tells us:

There is enormous natural variation in spinal curvature, pelvic position, and segmental alignment across healthy, pain-free individuals. What looks like “excessive kyphosis” or “anterior pelvic tilt” on visual inspection may simply be that person’s normal anatomy.
The relationship between static postural deviations and pain or injury is weak and inconsistent in the research literature. Many people with pronounced postural “faults” are completely asymptomatic, and many people with textbook-perfect alignment experience chronic pain.
The inter-rater reliability of visual postural assessment is generally poor. Two experienced practitioners observing the same person frequently disagree on the presence and severity of deviations.
Emerging technology may help address the reliability problem. For example, Roggio et al. (2024) demonstrated that machine learning-based pose estimation (using MediaPipe) achieved ICC values ranging from 0.67 to 0.95 for various postural parameters when assessed in healthy adults — substantially better than typical inter-rater agreement for visual observation alone.

What this means for your practice as an AES:

Postural observation is useful as a starting point for conversation, not as a diagnosis.
It can help you notice gross asymmetries or structural features worth exploring further, and it can inform exercise selection (e.g., someone presenting with a heavily flexed thoracic posture may benefit from extension-based mobility work).
Beyond cases with clear clinical significance (e.g., significant scoliosis, obvious structural deformity that warrants medical referral), avoid over-interpreting or over-extrapolating postural findings.
An AES does not diagnose postural pathology. If you observe something that concerns you — for example, a pronounced lateral curvature that the client is unaware of — your role is to note it and refer appropriately.



8.4.2 Activity 2.1: Basic Postural Observation
Working in pairs, conduct a brief standing postural observation of your partner from the anterior, posterior, and lateral views. Keep it simple and focus on the following:
Anterior view: - General symmetry: are the shoulders level? Is the head centred? - Position of the knees: any obvious valgus or varus alignment?
Posterior view: - Shoulder and scapular symmetry - Spinal alignment: any obvious lateral deviation? - Pelvic symmetry: are the iliac crests level?
Lateral view: - Head position relative to the shoulder (forward head posture?) - Thoracic curvature: within a range you would consider typical, or notably pronounced? - Lumbar curvature: as above - Knee position: hyperextension?
Record your observations using descriptive language rather than diagnostic labels. For example: “Shoulders appear slightly uneven, with the right sitting approximately 1–2 cm higher than the left” rather than “right upper trapezius hypertonia.”
Discussion questions:

How confident are you in your observations? Would your partner score the same things if they assessed you?
Would you change anything about this person’s exercise program based solely on what you observed? Why or why not?
At what point would a postural finding prompt you to refer to another professional? What would that referral look like?
How might technology (e.g., camera-based pose estimation as described by Roggio et al., 2024) change how we approach this assessment? What would it do better than the naked eye? What might it still miss?

title: 7  Week 11 - Practical
section: 8.5 Part 3: Dynamic Movement Assessment — Design Challenge (45–60 minutes)
text:
8.5 Part 3: Dynamic Movement Assessment — Design Challenge (45–60 minutes)

8.5.1 Background
This is the core of the lab. Rather than simply following a prescribed movement screening protocol, you are tasked with designing your own general movement screening document suitable for an apparently healthy adult client presenting for an initial assessment with an AES.
Dynamic movement assessment aims to observe how a person moves under load, through range, and across different planes of motion. Unlike static postural observation, it provides information about motor control, coordination, strength through range, and functional capacity — all of which are arguably more relevant to exercise prescription than standing alignment.
There are many established movement screening protocols (e.g., the Functional Movement Screen, the Bunkie test, various overhead and single-leg squat protocols), but no single test battery is universally accepted. Your task is to think critically about what movements you would include, what you are looking for in each one, and how you would record your findings.


8.5.2 Key Principles to Guide Your Design
When selecting movements for your screening, consider:

What are you actually assessing? Every movement you include should have a clear purpose. Are you looking at mobility? Stability? Motor control? Strength? Be specific.
What are the observation criteria? It is not enough to say “do a squat.” You need to define what you are looking for. For example, during an overhead squat, you might observe:

Can the client maintain an upright trunk position, or do they excessively flex forward?
Do the heels stay on the ground (ankle dorsiflexion)?
Do the knees track over the toes, or do they collapse inward (knee valgus)?
Can the arms stay overhead, or do they fall forward (thoracic extension and shoulder flexion range)?

What planes of movement are represented? A good screening should include movements that challenge sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. A battery consisting solely of squats and lunges (sagittal dominant) will miss important information about lateral stability and rotational control.
Is it practical? Consider time, equipment, and client comfort. A screening that takes 45 minutes and requires specialised equipment is unlikely to be used in practice.
How will you score or record findings? Will you use a numerical scale (e.g., 0–3 like the FMS)? A pass/fail system? Descriptive notes? A combination? Think about what is most useful for informing exercise prescription rather than generating a single composite number.



8.5.3 Example Dynamic Assessments
The following are examples of commonly used dynamic assessments. These are provided as a starting point — you do not need to include all of them, and you may choose others. The critical thing is that for each movement you select, you can articulate what you are looking for and why.
Overhead Squat - Purpose: Assesses bilateral lower limb mobility and stability, trunk control, and upper body mobility simultaneously. - What to observe: Depth achieved, trunk angle, heel position, knee tracking, arm position. - Limitations: Performance can be limited by ankle dorsiflexion, hip structure, or unfamiliarity with the pattern rather than a meaningful “dysfunction.”
Single-Leg Squat - Purpose: Assesses unilateral lower limb control, particularly hip-knee-ankle alignment in the frontal plane. - What to observe: Pelvic stability (Trendelenburg sign), knee valgus, trunk lateral flexion, depth and control. - Considerations: This is a challenging task — poor performance may reflect lack of practice or strength rather than pathology.
Active Straight-Leg Raise - Purpose: Assesses hamstring and hip flexor flexibility, and pelvic stability. - What to observe: Range of hip flexion achieved with a straight leg, movement of the contralateral limb and pelvis. - How to quantify: Can be measured with a goniometer or inclinometer, or estimated visually relative to anatomical landmarks.
Shoulder Mobility Assessment - Purpose: Assesses combined shoulder flexion/extension, internal/external rotation, and scapular mobility. - What to observe: Can the client reach behind their back with one hand from above and below simultaneously? Is there a notable asymmetry between sides? - Considerations: Structural differences (e.g., prior shoulder surgery, anatomical variation in the acromion) can influence this test independently of “mobility.”
Push-Up / Trunk Stability Assessment - Purpose: Assesses trunk stability and upper body pressing strength. - What to observe: Can the client maintain a neutral spine during the movement? Is there excessive lumbar extension or hip sag?
Single-Leg Balance / Modified Star Excursion - Purpose: Assesses balance, proprioception, and lower limb stability. - What to observe: Reach distance in multiple directions, stability of the stance leg, compensatory trunk movements.


8.5.4 Activity 3.1: Design Your Screening Document
In small groups (2–3 students), design a one-page movement screening document that includes:

3–5 dynamic movements you would include in a general screening for an apparently healthy adult.
For each movement, specify:

What you are assessing (the purpose)
What you are looking for (observation criteria — be specific)
How you will record findings (scoring system or descriptive method)

A brief rationale for your overall selection — why these movements? What do they cover collectively?

Be prepared to present and justify your choices to the class.


8.5.5 Activity 3.2: Perform Your Screening
Once your document is designed, use it. Have one group member perform the screening on another, with the third observing and providing feedback on the process. Rotate roles.
Debrief questions: - Was your scoring system practical and easy to use in real time? - Did you find yourself wanting to include additional observations that weren’t on your form? - How long did the screening take? Is that practical for a real-world initial assessment? - Where did you find the most disagreement between observers? What does that tell you about the reliability of your screening?

title: 7  Week 11 - Practical
section: 8.6 Part 4: Flexibility and Range of Motion (20–30 minutes)
text:
8.6 Part 4: Flexibility and Range of Motion (20–30 minutes)

8.6.1 Background
Flexibility and joint range of motion (ROM) assessment is a core competency within ESSA’s Exercise Science standards. Unlike postural observation, ROM measurement with appropriate tools (goniometer, inclinometer) provides quantifiable data that can be compared to normative values, tracked over time, and used to inform targeted exercise prescription.
Key principles:

Standardisation matters. The value of ROM measurement depends on consistent procedures: client positioning, landmark identification, stabilisation of proximal segments, and tester experience.
Active vs. passive ROM. Active ROM (client moves themselves) reflects their functional range and willingness to move. Passive ROM (tester applies the movement) reflects the structural capacity of the joint. Both provide useful but different information.
Bilateral comparison. Comparing left to right is often more informative than comparing to population norms. A 10° side-to-side difference may be more clinically relevant than being 5° below a normative average.

Have two different testers measure the same joint on the same person. Compare results. Discuss:

What are the sources of error (landmark identification, reading the goniometer, client positioning, client effort)?
How could you improve consistency?



8.6.4 Connecting ROM to Your Movement Screening
Consider how the ROM data you collected relates to the dynamic movement findings from Part 3. For example:

Did limited ankle dorsiflexion on goniometry correspond with heel rise during the overhead squat?
Did reduced hip flexion ROM correspond with compensatory lumbar flexion during the active straight-leg raise?
Does this information change how you would prescribe exercise for this client?

title: 7  Week 11 - Practical
section: 8.7 Part 5: Technology-Assisted Assessment — Discussion and Demonstration (15–20 minutes, optional)
text:
8.7 Part 5: Technology-Assisted Assessment — Discussion and Demonstration (15–20 minutes, optional)

8.7.1 The Emerging Role of Computer Vision
Traditional movement assessment relies on the practitioner’s eye — and as you have likely discovered during this lab, visual observation is subjective and its reliability is limited. Emerging technology offers the possibility of more objective, repeatable measurement using nothing more than a standard camera.
How it works: Machine learning models such as MediaPipe (Google), OpenPose, and MoveNet can detect anatomical landmarks from a standard 2D video or photo feed. Once landmarks are identified, joint angles can be calculated automatically in real time. This means a practitioner could, in principle, set up a webcam, have a client perform a squat, and receive instant quantified data on knee flexion angle, trunk lean, ankle dorsiflexion, and more — without markers, without a goniometer, and without expensive motion capture equipment.
What the research shows:

Roggio et al. (2024) photographed 200 healthy adults from frontal, dorsal, and lateral views and used MediaPipe to extract 33 anatomical landmarks and calculate joint angles, body segment inclinations, and vector lengths. They reported ICC values up to 0.95 for test-retest reliability, suggesting the method is substantially more reproducible than visual inspection.
Their principal component and cluster analyses also revealed patterns in the data (e.g., distinct postural “types” based on shoulder-hip width differential and limb segment lengths) that visual observation alone would not have identified — demonstrating the potential for technology to go beyond simple measurement toward pattern recognition.
Other research has validated MediaPipe for measuring joint angles during squats, lunges, and other functional movements, with mean absolute errors within clinically acceptable ranges for sagittal plane measurements.

Current limitations:

Frontal plane measurements (e.g., knee valgus) are less reliable from a single 2D camera and benefit from a second camera angle.
Fast movements and transitions can introduce tracking errors, particularly at standard frame rates (30 fps).
The technology measures joint angles and positions — it does not interpret them. A computer can tell you the knee flexion angle is 85°, but it cannot tell you whether that is a problem for this particular client. Clinical reasoning remains a human task.

Discussion questions:

If you had access to a pose estimation tool in your practice, how would you use it? Would it replace any of the assessments you performed today, or complement them?
What are the advantages of having quantified angle data versus your visual observation notes from Part 3?
What are the risks of over-relying on technology-generated numbers without clinical context?
How might this technology change the way exercise scientists work over the next 5–10 years?

8.8 Summary and Key Takeaways

Pre-screening is non-negotiable. The APSS is the Australian industry standard. Administer it thoroughly, use it as a conversation starter, and know when to refer.
Static postural observation has a place, but a narrow one. Use it to notice, not to diagnose. Be honest about its limitations with yourself and your clients. Remember the scope of an AES — you screen and assess, you do not diagnose.
Dynamic movement assessment is more informative than static observation for exercise prescription purposes. The key is knowing what you are looking for in each movement and why.
Flexibility and ROM measurement provides quantifiable data that complements your qualitative movement observations. Standardised measurement with appropriate tools is more reliable and more useful than visual estimation alone.
Technology is rapidly changing this space. Camera-based pose estimation is already reliable enough for many screening applications and will continue to improve. Understanding these tools, their capabilities, and their limitations is part of being a contemporary exercise scientist.
Critical thinking matters more than any single protocol. There is no universally “correct” movement screening battery. What matters is that you can justify your assessment choices, articulate what you are observing, interpret findings within appropriate scope, and use the information to inform safe and effective exercise prescription.

text:
7.3 Part 2: Postural Observation
PLEASE SEE ESSA STUDENT MANUAL BOOK CHAPTER 8. “Static and Dynamic Posture” for more information.






DEFINITIONS






Anatomical position: the erect position of the body with the face directed forwards, the arms at the side of the body, toes and palms of the hands facing forwards. Used as a reference to describe the relationship of body segments to one another.
Centre of mass: a hypothetical point around which the force of gravity appears to act and at which the combined mass of the body appears to be concentrated. In humans in the anatomical position, it is approximately anterior to the second sacral vertebra. The location changes with every new position of the body and limbs.
Base of support (BoS): refers to the area beneath the person that is in contact with the supporting surface (i.e. in standing it is the feet and any other device in contact with the ground, e.g. crutches or walking sticks). It will vary in different positions (i.e. in sitting it would also include the chair).
Dynamic posture: the alignment of the body segments during movement.
Grid rating frame: a frame designed to provide visual cues of an individual’s posture to aid in correcting deviations.
Inclinometer: a device for measuring the angle of inclination of a body part.
Plumb line: a line (e.g. string) with a weight at one end (e.g. plumb bob) that is used to determine verticality.
Kinaesthetic: a conscious awareness of body position, muscle movement and mass as felt through nerve endings.
Kyphosis: excessive outward curvature of the spine.
Lordosis: excessive inward curvature of the spine.
Anterior pelvic tilt: the top of the pelvis rotates forward, increasing lumbar lordosis (looks like the pelvis “tipping down” at the front).
Posterior pelvic tilt: the top of the pelvis rotates backward, flattening lumbar lordosis (looks like the pelvis “tucking under”).
Genu recurvatum: hyperextension of the knee beyond neutral (looks like the knees “pushing backwards”).
Postural malalignment: differences in alignment between the left and right sides of the body and/or the front and back of the body.
Postural sway: horizontal movement around the centre of gravity.
Scoliosis: excessive lateral curvature of the spine.
Static posture: the alignment of the body while stationary.
Valgus: The part of the limb below the joint moves outward, making the joint look like it’s collapsing inward (knock‑kneed).
Varus: The part of the limb below the joint moves inward, making the joint look like it’s bowing outward (bow‑legged).




Observe your partner in standing from the front, back, and side.
Your task is to describe what you see, not to diagnose. Use specific, observable language rather than clinical labels. For example:







Instead of…
Try…




“Excessive kyphosis”
“The thoracic curve appears more pronounced than typical when viewed from the side”


“Anterior pelvic tilt”
“The pelvis appears to be tilted forward relative to the trunk, with the lower back showing a more pronounced curve”


“Right upper trap hypertonia”
“The right shoulder sits approximately 1-2 cm higher than the left”



What to look at:

Front: Are the shoulders level? Is the head centred? Any obvious knee valgus/varus?
Back: Shoulder and scapular symmetry. Any visible lateral spinal deviation? Are the iliac crests level?
Side: Head position relative to the shoulder. Thoracic and lumbar curvature. Knee position (hyperextended?).

Important caveats to remember:

There is enormous natural variation in posture across healthy, pain-free people. A “deviation” from a textbook ideal is not necessarily a problem.
The evidence linking static postural findings to pain or injury is weak and inconsistent.
Visual postural assessment has poor inter-rater reliability – two practitioners often disagree.
Beyond clearly significant findings (e.g., obvious scoliosis, major structural asymmetry), avoid over-interpreting. Your role as an AES is to notice and describe, not to diagnose.
If something concerns you, note it and refer appropriately.

Discussion: Compare your observations with a partner who assessed the same person. Where did you agree? Where did you disagree? What does that tell you about the reliability of this assessment method?

text:
7.4 Part 3: Static Flexibility Assessment
Perform the following flexibility tests on your partner. For each test, record your findings and compare bilaterally where applicable.

7.4.1 3.1 Sit and Reach

Purpose: Combined hamstring and lower-back flexibility.
Protocol: Client sits with legs extended, feet flat against the box. They reach forward along the scale as far as possible, holding for 2 seconds. Record the best of 3 trials.
Equipment: Sit-and-reach box.
Normative reference: Males approximately 20-30 cm; Females approximately 23-33 cm (varies by protocol and age). Below approximately 15 cm is generally considered below average.
Watch for: Knees bending (invalidates the test), bouncing at end range, excessive thoracic rounding compensating for limited hamstring length.



7.4.2 3.2 Thomas Test

Purpose: Hip flexor length – specifically the one-joint hip flexors (iliopsoas).
Protocol: Client sits at the end of the plinth with their gluteal fold at the edge. They lie back, pulling both knees to the chest to flatten the lumbar spine, then release the test leg to hang freely.
Equipment: Plinth at appropriate height. Goniometer or inclinometer app optional.

Qualitative scoring:

Negative (normal): Test thigh rests in line with the table surface or the hip reaches neutral/slight extension with the pelvis controlled.
Positive (restricted): Test thigh lifts off the table or the hip remains flexed above horizontal.
Compensations to note: Lumbar extension (back arching off table), anterior pelvic tilt, thigh abduction or external rotation.
Compare left vs. right.

Video: Thomas test https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NMDd-4NspHs


7.4.3 3.3 Kendall Test (Modified Thomas for Rectus Femoris)

Purpose: Rectus femoris (two-joint hip flexor) length. This is performed in conjunction with the Thomas test to differentiate between one-joint and two-joint hip flexor tightness.
Protocol: In the same modified Thomas position, observe the degree of knee flexion in the hanging test leg. A tight rectus femoris will limit knee flexion because it is stretched across both the hip and knee joints simultaneously.
Equipment: Same setup as the Thomas test.

Qualitative scoring:

Negative (normal): The hanging knee remains flexed, commonly around 80-90 degrees.
Positive (restricted): The test-side knee extends (straightens) as the hip is held in the modified Thomas position, suggesting rectus femoris tightness.
Compare left vs. right. Often performed and reported alongside the Thomas test as a combined assessment.

Video: Kendall test https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n8zRF56N-U8


7.4.4 3.4 Back Scratch Test

Purpose: Combined shoulder flexion/external rotation (reaching over) and extension/internal rotation (reaching behind).
Protocol: Client reaches one hand over the same shoulder and the other hand behind the back from below. Measure the distance between the middle fingertips. Positive score means fingers overlap; negative score means there is a gap.
Equipment: Tape measure or ruler.
Normative reference: Males approximately -5 to 0 cm; Females approximately 0 to +3 cm. Asymmetry greater than 3-4 cm between sides is notable.

Qualitative scoring:

Good: Fingers overlap.
Neutral: Fingers touch.
Limited: Gap between fingers.
Compare sides and note any pain or compensation (particularly trunk lateral flexion to close the gap). Note which component is more limited – the overhead reach (flexion/external rotation) or the behind-back reach (extension/internal rotation).

Video: Back scratch test https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=60hR4F4cjic


7.4.5 3.5 Weight-Bearing Lunge Test (Knee-to-Wall)

Purpose: Weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion range of motion.
Protocol: Client places their foot a set distance from a wall and lunges the knee forward toward the wall, keeping the heel on the ground. Measure the maximum distance from the great toe to the wall (cm) at the point where the knee can just touch the wall with the heel still down.
Equipment: Wall, tape measure.
Normative reference: Approximately 10-12 cm toe-to-wall distance. Side-to-side difference greater than 1.5-2 cm is notable and very common post-ankle sprain.

Qualitative scoring:

Pass at a given distance: Knee reaches the wall without heel lift, foot collapse, or knee valgus.
Restricted: Heel lifts before the knee reaches the wall, knee cannot touch the wall at a reasonable distance, pain occurs, or there is a large asymmetry between sides.
Ask the client whether they feel a “bony block” at the front of the ankle versus a muscular stretch in the calf – these suggest different limiting structures.

Video: WBLT https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U7woPNLUT3Q


7.4.6 3.6 Passive Straight Leg Raise

Purpose: Hamstring length. Also has a neurodynamic component if symptoms are reproduced.
Protocol: Client lies supine with both legs extended. The tester passively raises one leg (keeping the knee extended) until firm resistance is felt or the pelvis begins to rotate posteriorly.
Equipment: Goniometer or inclinometer app for precise measurement. If neither is available, use the subjective scoring scale below.
Normative reference: Approximately 70-90 degrees of hip flexion with knee extended. Below 70 degrees is generally considered limited.

Qualitative scoring:

Flexibility context: Restricted if there is lower ROM or clear asymmetry between sides.
Neurodynamic context: Positive if familiar buttock, leg, or radicular pain is reproduced – not just a hamstring stretch sensation.
Watch for: Pelvic rotation (mark where rotation begins – this is the true endpoint, not the forced maximum), contralateral leg lifting, knee bending. Note whether the stretch sensation is in the posterior thigh (hamstrings) or behind the knee (may indicate neural tension). Compare bilaterally.

Subjective scoring scale (if no goniometer/inclinometer available):







Score
Description




1 - Limited
Leg does not reach 45 degrees from horizontal. Notably restricted hamstring length.


2 - Moderate
Leg reaches approximately 45-70 degrees from horizontal. Some limitation present.


3 - Normal
Leg reaches approximately 70-90 degrees from horizontal. Within expected range.


4 - Above average
Leg easily exceeds 90 degrees (vertical) with no pelvic compensation.



Video: PSLR test https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ulTens_-7Q


7.4.7 3.7 MHFAKE Test (Maximal Hip Flexion Active Knee Extension)

Purpose: Hamstring length assessed under maximal hip flexion – more sport-specific than the passive SLR, commonly used in running and team-sport settings for hamstring assessment and return-to-sport monitoring.
Protocol: Client lies supine and pulls one hip into maximal flexion using their hands (thigh to chest). From this position, they actively extend the knee as far as possible. The angle of knee extension deficit from full extension (0 degrees) is measured.
Equipment: Goniometer or inclinometer app placed on the shin. If neither is available, use the subjective scoring scale below.
Normative reference: The closer to 0 degrees (full extension), the better the hamstring flexibility. Greater than 20-25 degrees deficit is generally considered limited.

Qualitative scoring:

Compare left and right – bilateral comparison is particularly important for this test.
Note pain, stretch tolerance, apprehension, or pelvic/lumbar compensation.
Mark as restricted if there is a clear side-to-side loss of range or if extension is pain-limited.
Watch for: Client losing maximal hip flexion during the knee extension (the hip must stay fully flexed throughout), contralateral leg lifting, and the location of the stretch sensation – posterior thigh (hamstrings) vs. behind the knee (neural tension).

Subjective scoring scale (if no goniometer/inclinometer available):







Score
Description




1 - Limited
Knee remains notably bent (greater than 30 degrees from full extension). Shin clearly angled away from vertical.


2 - Moderate
Knee approaches but does not reach full extension (approximately 15-30 degree deficit).


3 - Normal
Knee reaches within approximately 10-15 degrees of full extension. Shin is close to vertical.


4 - Above average
Knee reaches full or near-full extension (less than 10 degree deficit) with hip held in maximal flexion).



Video: MHFAKE Test https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KEMj1oYGFEg


7.4.8 Measurement Tools: Inclinometer vs. Goniometer
A goniometer measures the angle between two body segments at a joint. A plastic goniometer has two arms you align along each segment, with the pivot over the joint axis.
An inclinometer measures the angle of a single segment relative to gravity (vertical or horizontal). Your phone is essentially an inclinometer – its accelerometer detects tilt.
For the passive SLR and MHFAKE, either tool works: the inclinometer app placed on the shin gives you the angle directly. For the Thomas test, an inclinometer on the thigh tells you whether it is above or below horizontal.
If you do not have a goniometer or inclinometer, the subjective scoring scales above give you a practical alternative – and comparing your subjective scores against a partner who used a goniometer on the same person makes for a useful discussion about measurement precision.

title: 7  Practical: Pre-Screening, Postural Observation, Flexibility & Movement Assessment
text:
7.5 Part 4: Dynamic Movement Assessment (30-40 min)

7.5.1 Design Challenge
Rather than following a prescribed screening protocol, your task is to design a short movement screening suitable for an apparently healthy adult. Select 3-5 dynamic movements and, for each one, specify:

What you are assessing (the purpose)
What you are looking for (specific observation criteria)
How you will record your findings (scoring or descriptive)



7.5.2 Key Principles

Every movement you include should have a clear purpose. “Do a squat” is not enough – you need to define what you are observing.
Include movements across different planes (sagittal, frontal, transverse). A battery of only squats and lunges will miss lateral stability and rotational control.
Keep it practical – if it takes 30 minutes and requires specialised equipment, it will not get used.
Think about what is most useful for informing exercise prescription rather than generating a single composite score.



7.5.3 Example Movements to Consider
Overhead squat: Bilateral lower limb mobility and stability, trunk control, upper body mobility. Look at: depth, trunk angle, heel position, knee tracking, arm position. Consider: performance can be limited by ankle dorsiflexion, hip structure, or unfamiliarity rather than a meaningful dysfunction.
Single-leg squat: Unilateral lower limb control, particularly frontal plane hip-knee-ankle alignment. Look at: pelvic drop (Trendelenburg), knee valgus, trunk lean, depth and control. Consider: this is a challenging task – poor performance may reflect lack of practice rather than pathology.






Tip





Single-leg squat




Shoulder mobility reach: Combined shoulder flexion/extension and internal/external rotation. Look at: distance between hands (similar to the back scratch test but observed dynamically), asymmetry between sides.
Push-up or trunk stability assessment: Trunk stability under load. Look at: ability to maintain a neutral spine, excessive lumbar extension or hip sag.
Single-leg balance or modified star excursion: Balance, proprioception, lower limb stability. Look at: reach distance in multiple directions, stability of the stance leg, compensatory trunk movements.
These are examples – you may choose others. The critical thing is that you can justify your choices and articulate what you are observing and why.


7.5.4 Activity

In small groups, design your screening document.
Administer it on a partner. A third person observes and gives feedback.
Rotate roles.

Debrief: Was your scoring system practical in real time? How long did the screening take? Where was there the most disagreement between observers? What would you change?
